cards.q: Define a Brønsted–Lowry acid and a Brønsted–Lowry base.
cards.a:
An acid is a proton donor.
A base is a proton acceptor.
cards.why: The “proton” is an \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ion: a hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron.

cards.q: In aqueous solution, what does an acid such as \(\mathrm{HCl}\) actually do to the water?
cards.a: It donates a proton to a water molecule, forming the oxonium ion: \(\mathrm{HCl(aq) + H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow H_{3}O^{+}(aq) + Cl^{-}(aq)}\)
cards.why: \(\mathrm{H^{+}(aq)}\) is shorthand for \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}(aq)}\); acid–base reactions are proton transfers.

cards.q: What is a conjugate acid–base pair?
cards.a: Two species that differ by one proton, \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\). The acid has the extra proton; its conjugate base is what is left when it has donated it.
cards.why: For example \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COO^{-}}\), or \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\).

cards.q: Identify the two conjugate acid–base pairs in: \(\mathrm{NH_{3}(aq) + H_{2}O(l) \rightleftharpoons NH_{4}^{+}(aq) + OH^{-}(aq)}\)
cards.a:
Pair 1: \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) (acid) and \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) (base).
Pair 2: \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) (acid) and \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) (base).
cards.why: Here water donates a proton to ammonia, so water is acting as an acid.

cards.q: In the mixture used for nitration, \(\mathrm{HNO_{3} + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightleftharpoons H_{2}NO_{3}^{+} + HSO_{4}^{-}}\). Which species is the acid and which is the base? Name the conjugate pairs.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\) is the acid; \(\mathrm{HNO_{3}}\) is the base.
Pairs: \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}/HSO_{4}^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}NO_{3}^{+}/HNO_{3}}\).
cards.why: Whether a substance acts as an acid or a base depends on what it reacts with: sulfuric acid is the stronger proton donor.

cards.q: Why can water act as both a Brønsted–Lowry acid and a Brønsted–Lowry base? Give an example of each.
cards.a:
It can donate a proton (forming \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\)) or accept one (forming \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\)).
Acid: with \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\). Base: with \(\mathrm{HCl}\).
cards.why: A substance that can act as both is described as amphoteric (or amphiprotic).

cards.q: Define pH.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^{+}}]\)
cards.why: A logarithmic scale is used because \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) in aqueous solutions covers a very wide range, from about \(1\) to \(10^{-14}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).

cards.q: Calculate the pH of \(0.0250\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid.
cards.a: pH = 1.60
steps: \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is a strong acid, fully dissociated, so \([\mathrm{H^{+}}] = 0.0250\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).
cards.why: Give pH values to two decimal places.

cards.q: A sample of rainwater has pH 3.45. Calculate \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\).
cards.a: \(3.55 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: On a calculator: \(10^{x}\) of \(-3.45\).

cards.q: Calculate the pH of \(0.0500\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sulfuric acid, assuming it releases both of its protons completely.
cards.a: pH = 1.00
cards.why: For a diprotic strong acid, double the acid concentration before taking the log.

cards.q: By how much does \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) change when the pH falls by 1? By 2?
cards.a: A fall of 1 pH unit means \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) is 10 times greater; a fall of 2 means 100 times greater.
cards.why: pH is a log scale: each unit is a factor of 10 in hydrogen ion concentration.

cards.q: Show how the ionic product of water, \(K_{\text{w}}\), comes from the equilibrium constant for the dissociation of water.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{H_{2}O(l) \rightleftharpoons H^{+}(aq) + OH^{-}(aq)}\), so \(K_{\text{c}} = \frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{OH^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{H_{2}O}]}\).
Water is only slightly dissociated, so \([\mathrm{H_{2}O}]\) is effectively constant and is combined with \(K_{\text{c}}\): \(K_{\text{w}} = [\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{OH^{-}}]\).

cards.q: Define \(K_{\text{w}}\) and \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{w}}\), and give their values at 298 K.
cards.why: In pure water at 298 K, \([\mathrm{H^{+}}] = [\mathrm{OH^{-}}] = 1.00 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\), so the pH is 7.00.

cards.q: The dissociation of water is endothermic. Explain how \(K_{\text{w}}\) and the pH of pure water change as the temperature rises, and whether the water is still neutral.
cards.a: \(K_{\text{w}}\) increases, the pH of pure water falls below 7, but the water is still neutral.
marks: Raising the temperature shifts the endothermic equilibrium to the right.
So \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) and \([\mathrm{OH^{-}}]\) both increase, and \(K_{\text{w}}\) increases.
Higher \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) means a lower pH (below 7).
The water is still neutral because \([\mathrm{H^{+}}] = [\mathrm{OH^{-}}]\).

cards.q: At 50 °C, \(K_{\text{w}} = 5.48 \times 10^{-14}\ \text{mol}^{2}\,\text{dm}^{-6}\). Calculate the pH of pure water at this temperature.
cards.a: pH = 6.63
cards.why: pH 6.63 is neutral at 50 °C: neutral means equal concentrations of the two ions, not pH 7.

cards.q: Calculate the pH of \(0.150\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sodium hydroxide at 298 K.
cards.a: pH = 13.18
steps: \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is a strong base, fully dissociated: \([\mathrm{OH^{-}}] = 0.150\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).
cards.why: Strong base: find \([\mathrm{OH^{-}}]\), use \(K_{\text{w}}\) to find \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\), then the pH.

cards.q: Calculate the pH of \(0.0200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) barium hydroxide, \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_{2}}\), at 298 K.
cards.a: pH = 12.60
cards.why: Forgetting to double the hydroxide concentration gives 12.30, a common lost mark.

cards.q: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid.
cards.a: It is the degree of dissociation in water.
marks: A strong acid is (almost) completely dissociated into \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) and its anion in aqueous solution.
A weak acid is only slightly (partially) dissociated; the equilibrium lies well to the left.
For example, \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is strong; \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\) is weak.

cards.q: True or false: a strong acid and a concentrated acid mean the same thing.
cards.a: False. Strength is about how fully the acid dissociates; concentration is about how much acid is dissolved per dm³.
cards.why: You can have a dilute solution of a strong acid, or a concentrated solution of a weak acid.

cards.q: Why is aqueous ammonia described as a weak base? Write the equation.
cards.a:
Only a small fraction of the ammonia molecules accept a proton from water:
\(\mathrm{NH_{3}(aq) + H_{2}O(l) \rightleftharpoons NH_{4}^{+}(aq) + OH^{-}(aq)}\)
cards.why: The equilibrium lies well to the left, so the hydroxide ion concentration is much lower than the ammonia concentration.

cards.q: Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant, \(K_{\text{a}}\), of a weak acid \(\mathrm{HA}\). Give its units.
cards.a: \(K_{\text{a}} = \frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{A^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}\), units \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\).
cards.why: It comes from \(\mathrm{HA(aq) \rightleftharpoons H^{+}(aq) + A^{-}(aq)}\). A larger \(K_{\text{a}}\) means a stronger acid.

cards.q: Write the \(K_{\text{a}}\) expression for ethanoic acid, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\).
cards.a: \(K_{\text{a}} = \frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{CH_{3}COO^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}]}\)
cards.why: Water does not appear: it is the solvent and its concentration is effectively constant.

cards.q: Define \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\). Which is the stronger acid: one with \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}} = 3.8\) or one with \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}} = 4.8\)?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}} = -\log_{10}K_{\text{a}}\). The acid with \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}} = 3.8\) is stronger.
cards.why: A smaller \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\) means a larger \(K_{\text{a}}\), so the acid is more dissociated.

cards.q:
(a) Convert \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.35 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) into \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\).
(b) Convert \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}} = 3.75\) into \(K_{\text{a}}\).
cards.a:
(a) 4.87
(b) \(1.78 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\) has no units; \(K_{\text{a}}\) does.

cards.q: What two assumptions are made when calculating the pH of a weak acid HA from its concentration and Ka?
cards.a:
1. \([\mathrm{H^{+}}] = [\mathrm{A^{-}}]\): all the \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) comes from the acid (the dissociation of water is ignored).
2. \([\mathrm{HA}]_{\text{eq}} \approx [\mathrm{HA}]_{\text{initial}}\): so little dissociates that the acid concentration is unchanged.
cards.why: Together they give \(K_{\text{a}} = \frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}]^{2}}{[\mathrm{HA}]}\).

cards.q: Calculate the pH of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) ethanoic acid. \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).
cards.a: pH = 2.88
cards.why: Only about 1.3% of the acid molecules are dissociated, which justifies the assumptions.

cards.q: A \(0.0500\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) solution of a weak acid HA has pH 3.10. Calculate \(K_{\text{a}}\).
cards.a: \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.26 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: Keep the unrounded \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) in your calculator until the final answer.

cards.q: A solution of methanoic acid has pH 2.50. \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.78 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). Calculate the concentration of the acid.
cards.a: \(0.0562\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: Rearrange \(K_{\text{a}} = \frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}]^{2}}{[\mathrm{HA}]}\) for whichever quantity is unknown.

cards.q: Benzoic acid, used as a food preservative, has \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}} = 4.20\). Calculate the pH of a \(0.0200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) solution.
cards.a: pH = 2.95
cards.why: Convert \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\) to \(K_{\text{a}}\) first; never put \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\) straight into the expression.

cards.q: \(0.600\ \text{g}\) of ethanoic acid (\(M_{\text{r}} = 60.0\)) is dissolved in water and made up to \(250\ \text{cm}^{3}\). The pH is 3.08. Calculate \(K_{\text{a}}\).
cards.a: \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.73 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: First turn the mass into a concentration; then use the pH as for any weak acid.

cards.q: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid are each diluted by a factor of 10. Explain why the pH of the hydrochloric acid rises by 1 but the pH of the ethanoic acid rises by only about 0.5.
cards.a: Diluting a weak acid shifts its equilibrium towards dissociation, partly offsetting the dilution.
marks: HCl is fully dissociated, so \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) falls by a factor of 10 and the pH rises by 1.
For a weak acid, \([\mathrm{H^{+}}] = \sqrt{K_{\text{a}}[\mathrm{HA}]}\), so \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) falls by only \(\sqrt{10}\).
\(\log_{10}\sqrt{10} = 0.5\), so the pH rises by about 0.5.
Dilution shifts the weak acid equilibrium to the right, so a greater fraction dissociates.

cards.q: Ethanoic acid (\(K_{\text{a}} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)) at \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) has pH 2.88. Calculate its pH after diluting 10 times.
cards.a: pH = 3.38
cards.why: A rise of 0.50: the pH of a weak acid changes by half as much as a strong acid on dilution.

cards.q: Equimolar \(0.1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) solutions are made of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COONa}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_{4}Cl}\). Is each neutral, acidic or alkaline?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{NaCl}\): neutral (pH 7).
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}COONa}\): slightly alkaline.
\(\mathrm{NH_{4}Cl}\): slightly acidic.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COO^{-}}\) is the conjugate base of a weak acid and accepts protons from water; \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) is the conjugate acid of a weak base and donates protons.

cards.q: Put in order of increasing pH: \(0.1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) solutions of \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), \(\mathrm{HCl}\), \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\).
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{CH_{3}COOH} < \mathrm{NH_{3}} < \mathrm{NaOH}\)
(about pH 1, 3, 11 and 13)
cards.why: Weak acids and weak bases are only slightly dissociated, so their pH is less extreme than strong ones of the same concentration.

cards.q: \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by \(21.40\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.0950\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: \(0.0813\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: Convert \(\text{cm}^{3}\) to \(\text{dm}^{3}\) by dividing by 1000.

cards.q: \(30.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is added to \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{NaOH}\). Calculate the pH of the mixture.
cards.a: pH = 2.04
cards.why: Use the total volume of the mixture, not the volume of acid alone.

cards.q: \(30.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is added to \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{HCl}\). Calculate the pH of the mixture at 298 K.
cards.a: pH = 11.96
cards.why: When the base is in excess, find \([\mathrm{OH^{-}}]\) first, then use \(K_{\text{w}}\).

cards.q: Describe the pH curve when 0.1 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is added to 25 cm³ of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid.
cards.a: Starts at pH 1, rises only slowly, then rises almost vertically from about pH 3 to pH 11 at 25 cm³ (equivalence point, pH 7), then levels off at about pH 13.
cards.why: Strong acid with strong base: the salt formed (NaCl) is neutral, so the equivalence point is at pH 7.

cards.q: Describe the pH curve when 0.1 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is added to 25 cm³ of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid.
cards.a: Starts at about pH 3, rises a little and then levels into a gently sloping buffer region; rises steeply from about pH 7 to 11, with the equivalence point at about pH 9 (at 25 cm³), then levels off at about pH 13.
cards.why: The salt formed, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COONa}\), is slightly alkaline, so the equivalence point is above 7.

cards.q: Describe the pH curve when 0.1 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is added to 25 cm³ of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ aqueous ammonia.
cards.a: Starts at about pH 11, falls gently through a buffer region, then falls steeply from about pH 7 to 3, with the equivalence point at about pH 5 (at 25 cm³), then levels off at about pH 1.
cards.why: The salt formed, \(\mathrm{NH_{4}Cl}\), is slightly acidic, so the equivalence point is below 7.

cards.q: What is distinctive about the pH curve for a weak acid titrated with a weak base, such as ethanoic acid with ammonia?
cards.a: There is no steep vertical section: the pH changes gradually through the equivalence point (near pH 7 for these two).
cards.why: Without a sharp jump, no indicator gives a clear end point; a pH meter is used instead.

cards.q: How does a pH curve show whether the acid being titrated is strong or weak?
cards.a: A weak acid starts at a higher pH (about 3 rather than 1) and shows a buffer region where the pH rises only gradually; its vertical section is shorter and starts higher (about pH 7).
cards.why: The equivalence volume depends only on the amount of acid, not its strength.

cards.q: How does an acid–base indicator work?
cards.a: It is a weak acid, \(\mathrm{HIn}\), whose undissociated form and conjugate base have different colours: \(\mathrm{HIn(aq) \rightleftharpoons H^{+}(aq) + In^{-}(aq)}\).
cards.why: Adding acid shifts the equilibrium left (colour of \(\mathrm{HIn}\)); adding alkali shifts it right (colour of \(\mathrm{In^{-}}\)). The end point is when \([\mathrm{HIn}] = [\mathrm{In^{-}}]\).

cards.q: How do you choose a suitable indicator for a titration from its pH curve?
cards.a: Choose an indicator whose colour change (pH range) lies completely within the vertical section of the curve.
cards.why: Then the whole colour change happens within a fraction of a drop of titrant, at the equivalence point.

cards.q: Methyl orange changes colour at about pH 3–4.5; phenolphthalein at about pH 8–10. Which is suitable for each titration: strong acid–strong base, weak acid–strong base, strong acid–weak base?
cards.a:
Strong acid–strong base: either.
Weak acid–strong base: phenolphthalein.
Strong acid–weak base: methyl orange.
cards.why: Each vertical section must contain the indicator’s range: about 3–11, 7–11 and 3–7 respectively.

cards.q: True or false: at the equivalence point of every acid–base titration the pH is 7.
cards.a: False. Only for a strong acid with a strong base.
cards.why: Weak acid–strong base gives pH above 7; strong acid–weak base gives pH below 7, because of the salt formed.

cards.q: Outline how to obtain a pH curve for the titration of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: Calibrate a pH meter with buffers of known pH. Pipette 25.0 cm³ of the acid into a beaker; add the alkali from a burette in small portions (1 cm³, then 0.1–0.2 cm³ near the end point), stirring and recording the pH after each addition. Plot pH against volume added.
cards.why: Smaller additions near the equivalence point capture the steep section accurately.

cards.q: Explain why the pH at the half-neutralisation point of a weak acid–strong base titration equals the \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\) of the acid.
cards.a: Half the acid has been converted to its salt, so \([\mathrm{HA}] = [\mathrm{A^{-}}]\).
marks: At half-neutralisation, half of the \(\mathrm{HA}\) has reacted to form \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\), so \([\mathrm{HA}] = [\mathrm{A^{-}}]\).
\(K_{\text{a}} = \frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{A^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}\), so the concentration terms cancel.
So \(K_{\text{a}} = [\mathrm{H^{+}}]\), and \(\mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}} = \mathrm{pH}\).

cards.q: In a titration of a weak acid with sodium hydroxide, the equivalence point is at \(24.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\). The pH after adding \(12.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) is 4.20. Calculate \(K_{\text{a}}\).
cards.a: \(K_{\text{a}} = 6.31 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
steps: \(12.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) is half the equivalence volume, so \(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}} = 4.20\).
cards.why: Read the equivalence volume from the curve first, then halve it.

cards.q: Describe a method to find \(K_{\text{a}}\) of a weak acid without plotting a full pH curve.
cards.a: Titrate \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of the acid with sodium hydroxide using phenolphthalein, to find the end point. Then add a further \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of the same acid to the neutralised solution and measure its pH with a calibrated pH meter.
cards.why: The mixture now holds equal amounts of \(\mathrm{HA}\) and \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\), so \(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_{\text{a}}\), and \(K_{\text{a}} = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}}\).

cards.q: What is a buffer solution?
cards.a: A solution that keeps an approximately constant pH when it is diluted or when small amounts of acid or base are added.
cards.why: The pH does change a little; a buffer resists change, it does not prevent it.

cards.q: What does an acidic buffer contain, and what does a basic buffer contain? Give an example of each.
cards.a:
Acidic: a weak acid and a salt of that acid, e.g. \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COONa}\).
Basic: a weak base and a salt of that base, e.g. \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_{4}Cl}\).
cards.why: Each contains a large reservoir of both partners of a conjugate acid–base pair.

cards.q: Explain how an ethanoic acid / sodium ethanoate buffer resists a change in pH when a small amount of acid or alkali is added.
cards.a: The equilibrium \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + CH_{3}COO^{-}}\) shifts to remove what is added.
marks: The buffer contains large amounts of \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COO^{-}}\) (from the salt).
Added \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COO^{-}}\) to form \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\); the equilibrium shifts left.
Added \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) (or with \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\)); more acid dissociates and the equilibrium shifts right.
The ratio \([\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}]/[\mathrm{CH_{3}COO^{-}}]\) hardly changes, so \([\mathrm{H^{+}}]\) and the pH stay almost constant.

cards.q: Explain how an ammonia / ammonium chloride buffer resists a change in pH.
cards.a: It contains large amounts of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\), which remove added acid and base.
marks: Added \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\): \(\mathrm{NH_{3} + H^{+} \rightarrow NH_{4}^{+}}\).
Added \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\): \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+} + OH^{-} \rightarrow NH_{3} + H_{2}O}\).
There is so much \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) that their ratio hardly changes, so the pH stays almost constant.

cards.q: What assumptions are made when calculating the pH of an acidic buffer?
cards.a:
\([\mathrm{HA}]\) equals the concentration of acid added (its dissociation is negligible).
\([\mathrm{A^{-}}]\) equals the concentration of salt added (all the \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\) comes from the fully dissociated salt).
cards.why: Then \([\mathrm{H^{+}}] = K_{\text{a}} \times \frac{[\mathrm{HA}]}{[\mathrm{A^{-}}]}\); in the same solution, the ratio of moles can be used.

cards.q: A buffer contains \(0.100\ \text{mol}\) of ethanoic acid and \(0.0500\ \text{mol}\) of sodium ethanoate in \(1.00\ \text{dm}^{3}\). \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). Calculate its pH.
cards.a: pH = 4.46
cards.why: More acid than salt gives a pH below the pKa (4.76).

cards.q: \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is added to \(50.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) ethanoic acid. \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). Calculate the pH of the buffer formed.
cards.a: pH = 4.28
cards.why: Partly neutralising a weak acid with a strong base is a common way to make a buffer.

cards.q: A buffer contains \(0.0100\ \text{mol}\) each of \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COONa}\) (pH 4.76). Calculate the pH after adding \(0.00100\ \text{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{HCl}\). \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).
cards.a: pH = 4.67
cards.why: The pH falls by only 0.09; the same acid added to water would change the pH by several units.

cards.q: The same buffer (\(0.0100\ \text{mol}\) each of \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COONa}\)) instead has \(0.00100\ \text{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) added. Calculate the new pH. \(K_{\text{a}} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).
cards.a: pH = 4.85
cards.why: Added base converts acid into its conjugate base, so the ratio shifts in favour of the salt.

cards.q: A buffer of pH 5.00 is needed, using \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) ethanoic acid (\(K_{\text{a}} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)). What concentration of sodium ethanoate is needed, and what mass of \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COONa}\) (\(M_{\text{r}} = 82.0\)) for \(500\ \text{cm}^{3}\)?
cards.a: \(0.174\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\); 7.13 g
cards.why: For a pH above the pKa (4.76), you need more salt than acid.

cards.q: Where on the pH curve for a weak acid titrated with a strong base is buffer action shown, and why?
cards.a: In the gently sloping region before the equivalence point, centred on half-neutralisation. Adding base there changes the pH only slowly.
cards.why: In that region the solution contains significant amounts of both \(\mathrm{HA}\) and \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\): it is a buffer.

cards.q: Give three applications of buffer solutions.
cards.a: Controlling the pH of blood; keeping the pH of shampoos, cosmetics and foods correct; and maintaining a steady pH in industrial processes such as fermentation and in calibrating pH meters.
cards.why: Enzymes, dyes and many products only work or stay stable within a narrow pH range.

cards.q: Explain how carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions keep the pH of blood close to 7.4.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H_{2}CO_{3}(aq) \rightleftharpoons H^{+}(aq) + HCO_{3}^{-}(aq)}\) acts as a buffer.
marks: Blood contains carbonic acid, \(\mathrm{H_{2}CO_{3}}\), and hydrogencarbonate ions, \(\mathrm{HCO_{3}^{-}}\).
Excess \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) (e.g. lactic acid in exercise) reacts with \(\mathrm{HCO_{3}^{-}}\) to form \(\mathrm{H_{2}CO_{3}}\).
Excess \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{H_{2}CO_{3}}\), forming \(\mathrm{HCO_{3}^{-}}\) and water.
\(\mathrm{H_{2}CO_{3}}\) is in equilibrium with dissolved \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), which is removed by breathing out, so the ratio stays nearly constant.

cards.q: True or false: a mixture of hydrochloric acid and sodium chloride is a buffer.
cards.a: False. A buffer needs a weak acid (or weak base) and its conjugate partner.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) is too weak a base to remove added \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), and HCl is fully dissociated so there is no reservoir of undissociated acid.

cards.q: Explain why the enthalpy change of neutralisation of a weak acid by sodium hydroxide is less exothermic than that of a strong acid.
cards.a: For strong acids it is about \(-57\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) in each case; for a weak acid some energy goes into dissociating it.
marks: For a strong acid, the reaction is just \(\mathrm{H^{+}(aq) + OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow H_{2}O(l)}\), so the value is almost the same for every strong acid.
A weak acid is only partially dissociated; as \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) is removed, more acid dissociates.
Dissociating the weak acid is endothermic (needs energy to break the O–H bond).
So less energy overall is released per mole of water formed.
